html:
The Constitution of Colombia of 1991 replaced the centralised Conservative constitution of 1886. It was written by an elected assembly that included former guerrillas of the M-19, which had laid down its arms.

A student movement had pushed for a new charter amid the violence of the cartel wars. The new constitution declared Colombia a social state under the rule of law, recognised its many ethnic groups and languages, gave land rights to Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities, and set up a Constitutional Court.

It also created the tutela, a quick court action any citizen can bring to defend basic rights, which millions have used to claim health care. It banned extradition, a concession to the traffickers later reversed. It is the framework of modern Colombia, and the peace deal of 2016 was built within it, after the long century of the civil wars.
